title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Depression — August 2026

studies.title: Autistic adults in the UK are twice as likely to be on antidepressants — and stay on them longer
studies.ns_score_reason: enormous, population-representative dataset and a stark, quotable gap; limited by the fact that prescribing records can't tell you whether the drugs are helping.
studies.the_study: Using UK primary care records from Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum spanning 1997–2023, researchers compared antidepressant prescribing in 172,242 autistic adults (47,011 with intellectual disability, 125,231 without) and 34.2 million non-autistic adults. In 2023, 30% of autistic adults received an antidepressant prescription versus 14.7% of non-autistic adults. Prescribing has risen faster in autistic people across the whole period, with more new starters, higher average doses of citalopram, fluoxetine and sertraline, and longer courses — course durations were longest in autistic adults with intellectual disability, the very group for whom depression and anxiety were least often recorded as the indication.
studies.why_it_matters: A large minority of autistic adults are on long-term SSRIs prescribed on an evidence base that was largely not built in autistic people, and in the intellectual disability group frequently without a recorded mental health indication at all.
studies.pitch_angle: Nearly one in three autistic adults in Britain was prescribed an antidepressant last year — a rate that has pulled away from the general population every year since 1997. Open on an autistic adult who has been on the same SSRI for five years without anyone revisiting the decision. Call Amir Sadik or Dhruv Rai at Bristol's MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit, and pair with an autistic self-advocate. Frame carefully: the data describe prescribing patterns, not whether the drugs work or harm.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health-policy or long-read outlet on the "diagnostic overshadowing" problem in reverse — what happens when a neurodevelopmental diagnosis becomes a route into decades of psychotropic medication, and why the trials that would settle the question have never been run in this group.
studies.caveats: Observational routine-care data (cannot establish causation or clinical appropriateness); autism ascertainment in primary care records is incomplete and likely skews toward later-diagnosed adults; no outcome data on symptoms, side effects or discontinuation.

studies.title: The eye may flag depression years early — but the layer is thicker, not thinner
studies.ns_score_reason: huge cohort plus Mendelian randomization, and the direction of effect contradicts the prevailing "retinal thinning" story; limited by the modest effect sizes typical of Biobank imaging work.
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed retinal optical coherence tomography from 23,225 UK Biobank participants, with brain MRI in a subset of 1,475, and ran Mendelian randomization using published GWAS data to probe causality. Thicker — not thinner — ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) predicted subsequent depression in Cox models, and the genetic analysis pointed the same way. Mediation analysis suggested a possible anatomical route from GCIPL thickness to depression-related brain regions via primary and secondary visual cortex volumes.
studies.why_it_matters: Much previous work assumed neurodegeneration-style retinal thinning in depression; if the true signal runs the other way, retinal screening for mood risk needs rethinking before anyone builds a clinical tool on it.
studies.pitch_angle: An eye scan you get at the optician may contain a signal about your mood years before you feel low — and the researchers found the opposite of what the field expected. Open on the ordinary experience of an OCT scan in a high-street eye test. Call Zhe Jin or Meixiao Shen at Wenzhou Medical University's Eye Hospital, and get an independent retinal-imaging skeptic to interrogate the reversal. Be explicit that nobody should read anything into their own scan.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist ophthalmology or medical-imaging outlet: the "oculomics" boom — retinal scans now being mined for Alzheimer's, cardiovascular risk, Parkinson's and now depression, and the replication crisis quietly building as different cohorts return contradictory directions of effect.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort (Mendelian randomization strengthens but does not prove causal inference); UK Biobank is older, whiter and healthier than the UK population; effect direction conflicts with prior literature and needs independent replication; mediation analysis is exploratory.

studies.title: Support groups in the metaverse underperform sitting in a room together
studies.ns_score_reason: a properly randomized three-arm test of a heavily hyped delivery format, with a largely null result for the shiny option; limited by attrition and modest power.
studies.the_study: 156 Ukrainian refugees in Romania were randomized to avatar-based virtual reality support groups, conventional in-person support groups, or a waitlist, with assessments at baseline, mid-point, post-intervention and three months. In-person groups produced the strongest short-term benefits — notably greater perceived social support versus waitlist, and reduced anxiety in end-point analyses. Avatar VR effects were smaller and did not reach significance, and most gains had faded by follow-up.
studies.why_it_matters: Immersive VR is being pitched as the scalable answer to psychosocial support in crisis settings; this is one of the first randomized head-to-head tests, and it does not deliver equivalence to the low-tech option.
studies.pitch_angle: The metaverse was supposed to bring group therapy to people who can't reach a clinic. Randomized against a room with chairs in it, the avatars lost. Open on a displaced Ukrainian woman putting on a headset in Bucharest. Call Cezar Giosan at the University of Bucharest, and Albert "Skip" Rizzo at USC — a long-standing VR-therapy advocate who is a co-author, which makes the null result more interesting, not less.
studies.wider_angle: For a technology or business outlet: the quiet contraction of clinical metaverse ventures, and what the evidence base actually shows for VR in mental health — strong for exposure therapy for specific phobias, thin to absent for social and relational interventions.
studies.caveats: Substantial attrition; clustering reduced effective power; short follow-up (3 months) with effects attenuating; population may not generalize beyond refugees with varying digital familiarity; findings are largely null rather than a demonstration of inferiority.

studies.title: Depression compresses the mental map of emotions
studies.ns_score_reason: large first sample, a second study with 14-day experience sampling, and an idea readers can immediately picture; limited by the key mediation effect vanishing after baseline adjustment.
studies.the_study: In Study 1, 1,311 people aged 8–25 rated how similar emotion words were and how likely one emotion was to follow another; researchers built low-dimensional emotion "spaces" and network models. Higher depression and anxiety symptoms went with a compressed emotion space, denser similarity networks with shorter path lengths, and higher transition probabilities between emotions. Study 2 (N=88, aged 18–23) replicated the pattern and added 14 days of experience sampling: depression was linked to rigid, congruent day-to-day emotional covariation, anxiety to unstable, incongruent patterns.
studies.why_it_matters: Most work on "emotional differentiation" has measured how people label feelings in the moment; this suggests the underlying conceptual architecture — what a person thinks the emotions *are* and how they relate — is itself flattened in depression, and that it can shift over weeks.
studies.pitch_angle: For someone who is depressed, "sad," "lonely," "empty" and "tired" may not just feel similar — they may literally occupy nearly the same point in the mind's map of feelings. Open on the everyday experience of not being able to say what you're feeling. Call Dongtao Wei or Jiang Qiu at Southwest University. Hook: the semantic network was measurably looser after two weeks of sampling, hinting the structure is plastic.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest or language-focused outlet on emotional granularity — Lisa Feldman Barrett's constructionist account, the "untranslatable emotions" literature, and whether teaching children a richer emotion vocabulary is a plausible mental health intervention or a just-so story.
studies.caveats: Study 2 N=88; the mediation pathway from emotional covariation to depressive symptom change disappeared after controlling for baseline BDI; self-reported symptoms throughout; both samples Chinese students, so cross-cultural generalization untested; cross-sectional in Study 1.

studies.title: Shame — not guilt — explains why teenage girls get more depressed than boys
studies.ns_score_reason: three waves, nearly 3,000 adolescents, and a clean dissociation between two emotions people routinely conflate; limited by all-self-report mediation modeling.
studies.the_study: 2,915 Chinese adolescents (mean age 17.0; 40% female) completed measures of shame proneness, guilt proneness, maladaptive cognitive emotion regulation and depressive symptoms across three waves over 12 months. Girls scored higher on all four. Shame significantly mediated the sex gap in depression; guilt did not. A serial pathway held: sex → shame → maladaptive emotion regulation → depressive symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: Shame and guilt are usually lumped together as "self-conscious emotions," but only one appears to drive the best-documented demographic gap in adolescent depression — which points interventions at a specific target rather than at negative self-evaluation in general.
studies.pitch_angle: Guilt is about what you did; shame is about what you are — and only the second one appears to be making teenage girls depressed. Open on a 16-year-old rehearsing an embarrassing moment for the hundredth time. Call Chun Huang or Debbie Wang at Wenzhou Medical University. Ask them directly whether shame-focused programs (compassion-focused therapy, for instance) have been trialed at this age.
studies.wider_angle: For an education or parenting outlet: what the shame/guilt distinction means for how schools handle discipline, social media incidents and academic failure — and why "you should be ashamed of yourself" may be worse advice than it sounds.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation, mediation models assume a causal ordering they cannot test); entirely self-reported; single-country sample with an unusual sex ratio (40% female); 12-month follow-up.

studies.title: Prolonged childhood loneliness roughly triples the odds of a first psychotic episode
studies.ns_score_reason: big multinational sample with genetic data and a genuine gene-environment interaction test; held back by retrospective recall of childhood loneliness in people who now have psychosis.
studies.the_study: Analyzing 2,565 participants (1,084 with first-episode psychosis, 1,481 controls) from the EU-GEI study, researchers asked about prolonged loneliness before age 12 and at 12–16, and calculated polygenic scores for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depression. Loneliness before 12 was associated with nearly triple the odds of first-episode psychosis (OR 2.90), independent of premorbid social isolation — meaning the feeling, not merely the lack of company. Adolescent loneliness was more strongly linked to affective psychosis, particularly in girls, and showed additive interaction with schizophrenia polygenic risk.
studies.why_it_matters: It separates subjective loneliness from objective isolation as a developmental risk marker, and offers evidence that early social-emotional experience amplifies inherited liability rather than acting alongside it.
studies.pitch_angle: Being alone and feeling alone are not the same thing — and it's the feeling that tracks psychosis risk, on top of genes. Open on the distinction: the child with friends who still feels unreachable. Call Covadonga Díaz-Caneja or Álvaro Andreu-Bernabeu at Gregorio Marañón in Madrid. Handle the gene-environment interaction carefully; the depression-PGS interaction did not survive the European-ancestry sensitivity analysis.
studies.wider_angle: For a policy or society outlet: the UK and other governments have loneliness strategies aimed almost entirely at older adults. This is part of a growing evidence base that the developmentally critical window is childhood — a "loneliness in schools" feature.
studies.caveats: Loneliness assessed retrospectively, creating recall bias in a diagnosed group; observational design; one interaction failed to replicate in ancestry-restricted analysis; several authors declare extensive pharmaceutical industry consultancy (Arango, Bobes, Díaz-Caneja — see disclosure list).

studies.title: Thirty-seven questions predict who will still be depressed or anxious two years later
studies.ns_score_reason: genuine external validation in a separate set of 13 colleges, which most prediction papers skip; limited by being confined to one intervention in US undergraduates.
studies.the_study: Researchers took undergraduates at risk of, or meeting criteria for, anxiety, depression or eating disorders who received digital guided self-help CBT, and used a five-step feature selection process to reduce 863 baseline questionnaire items to 37. Five machine learning algorithms were trained on students from 13 US colleges (n=1,472) and externally validated in 13 different colleges (n=823); random forest performed best on discrimination, calibration and clinical utility. Predictors of being disorder-free at two years included lower behavioral avoidance, less perseverative thinking, fewer worry topics, more feelings of calm — and, notably, higher perceived need for treatment and greater intention to seek help.
studies.why_it_matters: Most psychiatric prediction models are never validated outside their training data; this one was, and the result is a short self-report instrument that could triage students on campuses that cannot afford to treat everyone.
studies.pitch_angle: A 37-item questionnaire, sat at the start of a digital therapy program, can flag who will still be unwell two years later — and one of the strongest signals is simply whether the student thinks they need help. Open on a first-year filling in a wellbeing screener during freshers' week. Call Michelle Newman at Penn State or Denise Wilfley at Washington University. Resist the "AI predicts depression" framing; this is prediction of response, not diagnosis.
studies.wider_angle: For a higher-education or data-ethics outlet: universities are already screening students at scale. A piece on what happens when algorithmic triage arrives in campus counseling — consent, false positives, and whether being told you're high-risk is itself a nocebo.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of trial data; US undergraduates only, so generalization to other ages and health systems is unclear; predictors are all self-reported; the model predicts outcomes within a specific digital CBT program, not natural course; no evidence yet that acting on the algorithm improves outcomes.

studies.title: Gut bacteria in depression shift from fermenting sugars to fermenting protein
studies.ns_score_reason: a specific, testable metabolic signature rather than the usual vague "microbiome differences," with an AUC of 0.871; limited by cross-sectional design and a small control group.
studies.the_study: Fecal short-chain fatty acids and serum inflammatory markers were measured in 102 patients with major depressive disorder and 38 matched healthy controls. Patients showed depletion of straight-chain SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) and elevation of branched-chain SCFAs — the signature of gut bacteria switching from fermenting carbohydrate to fermenting protein. A combined model of branched-chain SCFAs, acetate, an acute phase inflammatory index and epidermal growth factor separated patients from controls with an AUC of 0.871, and the same markers tracked symptom severity, physiosomatic symptoms and number of past episodes.
studies.why_it_matters: It moves the gut-brain story in depression from "the microbiome differs" to a named metabolic switch with a plausible route to systemic inflammation — a hypothesis that can be tested with dietary fiber interventions.
studies.pitch_angle: The bacteria in the gut of someone with depression appear to have run out of fiber and started breaking down protein instead, generating compounds that track with inflammation and symptom severity. Open on the mundane fact of what most people actually eat. Call Michael Maes (UESTC Chengdu / Chulalongkorn) — a prolific and sometimes contested figure in immunopsychiatry, worth balancing with an independent microbiome researcher. Do not imply anyone should change their diet on this evidence.
studies.wider_angle: For a nutrition or food-science outlet: the fiber gap as a public health story. Branched-chain SCFAs are a well-known marker of low-fiber, high-protein diets in gastroenterology; this connects that literature to psychiatry for the first time in a clinical sample.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, so direction of causation is unknown — depression alters diet and appetite; only 38 controls; residual confounding by diet, BMI and smoking is hard to rule out; medication effects are noted (5-HT1A agents associated with higher branched-chain SCFAs); single center in Chengdu.

studies.title: Which psychotherapy works for anorexia may depend on how depressed you are
studies.ns_score_reason: a rare six-year follow-up from a multicenter RCT and a clean, actionable moderator; limited by being an explicit exploratory secondary analysis.
studies.the_study: The ANTOP trial randomized 242 adults with anorexia nervosa across 10 German university hospitals to focal psychodynamic therapy (FPT), enhanced CBT (CBT-E), or optimized treatment as usual, and found no BMI difference between arms. This secondary analysis of the 160 patients in the two active therapy arms, using mixed models with BMI at a mean 5.96 years of follow-up, found that low baseline depression severity and high mental quality of life favored CBT-E, while high depression severity and low mental quality of life favored FPT. The direction held at every earlier time point.
studies.why_it_matters: A headline "no difference between therapies" trial can conceal two treatments that work for different people — and this is exactly the kind of moderator analysis that turns a null RCT into a matching rule worth testing prospectively.
studies.pitch_angle: The trial said it didn't matter which therapy you got. Six years on, the data say it mattered a great deal — if you were also depressed. Open on the clinical coin-toss patients currently face when a service offers whichever therapy it happens to have. Call Beate Wild or Stephan Zipfel at Heidelberg/Tübingen. Frame as a hypothesis for a prospective matching trial, not a treatment rule.
studies.wider_angle: For a research-methods-literate outlet (or a Nature-style news feature): the "null trial" problem across psychotherapy research. Averages have dominated the field for decades; moderator analyses like this one are how precision psychiatry either arrives or fails to replicate.
studies.caveats: Exploratory secondary analysis, not pre-registered as a moderator test; N=160 across two arms is small for interaction effects; effects concentrated at the extremes of the depression and quality-of-life distributions, with a wide middle range where the therapies performed alike; German university hospital patients.

studies.title: Stress and low mood predict everyday aggression; political ideology doesn't
studies.ns_score_reason: a large community sample and a direct challenge to two dominant social-psychology predictors; limited by cross-sectional self-report and a single-country sample.
studies.the_study: In a community sample of 1,215 adults, the researcher regressed a brief index of *recent* aggressive acts on perceived stress, anxiety, depressive symptoms, social support, mentalizing ability (Reading the Mind in the Eyes), right-wing authoritarianism, social dominance orientation, and demographics. Stress, anxiety and depressive symptoms were each uniquely associated with aggression and the distress block explained the largest share of variance. Mentalizing and authoritarianism facets were not uniquely related; social dominance orientation showed a small *inverse* association, contrary to theory. Findings held under robust and quantile regression.
studies.why_it_matters: Two of the most heavily studied predictors of aggression in social psychology — ideological orientation and deficits in reading others' minds — did no work once current distress was in the model, at least for recently enacted aggression rather than trait questionnaires.
studies.pitch_angle: We keep explaining aggression with ideology and empathy deficits. In a sample of 1,215 adults, what actually predicted having hit, shoved or shouted at someone recently was how stressed, anxious and low the person was. Open on the ordinary domestic flashpoint. Call Oulmann Zerhouni at Université Paris Nanterre and press him on the anomalous social dominance finding, which he himself interprets cautiously.
studies.wider_angle: For a criminology or public-policy outlet: if proximal distress rather than disposition drives most everyday aggression, that argues for interventions aimed at stressors — debt, overcrowding, sleep, waiting lists — rather than at attitudes. A "prevention by economics" piece.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational (cannot establish causation); all measures self-reported, including the aggression index; French community sample only; null results for ideology may reflect measurement in a low-variance sample rather than absence of effect.

studies.title: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and the brain: the causal evidence isn't there yet
studies.ns_score_reason: a disciplined causal-inference framework applied to the most-discussed drug class of the decade; loses points for being a review rather than new data.
studies.the_study: The authors applied the Bradford Hill criteria for causal inference to the full spread of evidence on GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists — receptor pharmacology, preclinical work, RCTs, observational studies and pharmacovigilance databases — and assessed each reported neuropsychiatric outcome: depression, anxiety, suicidality, reward-related behavior, cognition, and ocular disturbance. Their conclusion is that biological plausibility exists for a relationship between these drugs and psychopathology, but the evidence is insufficient to establish causality for most outcomes.
studies.why_it_matters: Millions of people are now on these drugs and both the "Ozempic makes you suicidal" and "Ozempic cures addiction" narratives are running well ahead of the data; this is a structured account of exactly which claims have support and which do not.
studies.pitch_angle: Both the alarm and the enthusiasm about what semaglutide does to your mind fail the standard test for causation. Open on the sheer scale of exposure — a drug class taken by millions with no prospective psychiatric endpoint data. Call Fabrizio Schifano at the University of Hertfordshire, whose group specializes in pharmacovigilance signal detection, and ask which single trial would settle it.
studies.wider_angle: For a science-communication or medicine outlet: a case study in how pharmacovigilance databases generate headlines. Spontaneous adverse-event reporting is exquisitely sensitive to media coverage, producing feedback loops in which reporting drives reports. A piece on the epistemics of drug scares.
studies.caveats: Narrative/systematic review, not primary data; heterogeneous underlying evidence base; pharmacovigilance data are subject to severe reporting bias; the review cannot resolve confounding by indication (obesity and diabetes are themselves associated with depression).

studies.title: Rumination has no shared brain signature — everyone ruminates differently
studies.ns_score_reason: an honest, well-designed partial failure that says something real about individual variability; capped by N=24 and proof-of-principle framing.
studies.the_study: Twenty-four people with depression underwent six eight-minute inductions of either rumination or distraction across three sessions, with 64-channel EEG recorded throughout. Participant-specific support vector machines were trained on alpha, beta and theta power plus inter-channel connectivity. Averaged across participants, classification of ruminative state beat chance — but only slightly, and at the individual level just 10 of 24 participants had decoders that exceeded chance, with feature weights that differed markedly from person to person.
studies.why_it_matters: If rumination cannot be read off a common neural pattern, the ambition of closed-loop neurofeedback that detects and interrupts rumination in real time is much harder than it looks — and "rumination" may be a label covering several distinct processes.
studies.pitch_angle: Researchers tried to catch rumination in the act using EEG. It worked in fewer than half the participants, and the brain features that gave it away were different in each one. Open on the idea of a wearable that buzzes when you start spiraling — and why that device is further away than its backers claim. Call Jana Welkerling at Tübingen or Tim Rohe at FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg.
studies.wider_angle: For a technology outlet: the consumer neurofeedback market is selling headbands that claim to detect mental states. A reported piece on what EEG can and cannot decode from the scalp, using this study as the sober benchmark.
studies.caveats: Small N (24); single center; proof-of-principle with no clinical outcome; rumination induction is a laboratory proxy for spontaneous rumination; self-reported rumination levels as the ground truth; largely a negative result at the individual level.

studies.title: Growing up with a parent's drinking problem raises adult depression risk — but not on its own
studies.ns_score_reason: a careful meta-analysis whose most interesting finding is deflationary; the headline association itself is well established.
studies.the_study: A systematic review across Medline, PsycINFO, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library identified 32 eligible studies, 29 of which entered random-effects meta-analyses of childhood exposure to parental problematic alcohol use and adult mental health. Pooled effects showed a 73% higher likelihood of anxiety (SMD 0.37) and a 65% higher likelihood of depression (SMD 0.29). Effects were attenuated — though still significant — in studies adjusting for confounders, and the authors conclude that much of the association may reflect co-occurring childhood adversities and broader family dysfunction.
studies.why_it_matters: Adult children of alcoholics are often framed as a distinct clinical population with a specific inherited or environmental burden; the pooled evidence suggests parental drinking is better understood as one marker within a cluster of adversities rather than a standalone cause.
studies.pitch_angle: The "adult child of an alcoholic" is a fixed identity in self-help culture. A meta-analysis of 29 studies finds the mental health risk is real but substantially shared with other family adversity — which reframes what the risk actually is. Open on someone who has organized their self-understanding around a parent's drinking. Call Filipa Novais at the Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de Lisboa.
studies.wider_angle: For a general-interest or long-read outlet: how the adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) framework became ubiquitous in schools, social work and policy, and the growing methodological critique that individual ACEs rarely have independent effects once the others are accounted for.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of observational studies (cannot establish causation); heavy reliance on retrospective recall of childhood exposure; heterogeneity across 29 studies; publication bias not described in the abstract; residual confounding by genetics and socioeconomic position acknowledged by the authors.

studies.title: Preventing perinatal depression doesn't automatically make parents warmer
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean null on a widely assumed knock-on benefit, with direct observational coding rather than self-report; limited by sample size and a 42-month gap.
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 103 mother-child dyads from a longitudinal study of Mothers and Babies (MB), a cognitive-behavioral perinatal depression prevention program, compared with community home-visiting care as usual. At 42 months postpartum, verbal and physical expressions of parental warmth were coded from virtual observational assessments using the Brief Parent-Child Early Relational Assessment. There were no significant differences between groups in either the amount or the quality of warmth.
studies.why_it_matters: Perinatal depression prevention is often justified partly by presumed downstream benefits for the child through improved parenting; this suggests reducing maternal symptoms does not by itself transfer to warmer parenting three years later.
studies.pitch_angle: A program that reliably reduces perinatal depression left no detectable mark on how warm mothers were with their toddlers three years on. Open on the assumption everyone makes — treat the mother, and the parenting follows. Call S. Darius Tandon at Northwestern, who developed MB and published the null himself. Note the honest implication the authors draw: parenting may need to be targeted directly.
studies.wider_angle: For a public-health or early-years policy outlet: the "two-generation" logic underpinning huge amounts of maternal mental health investment worldwide, and what the evidence actually shows about whether treating parents changes child outcomes.
studies.caveats: Small N (103 dyads); substudy of an observational longitudinal study rather than the original randomized comparison; 42-month gap between intervention and assessment; virtual observational assessment may miss physical warmth; low-income, racially diverse US sample — a strength for equity but limits generalization; null result may reflect insufficient power.

studies.title: In fibromyalgia, depression and body-wide symptom burden multiply each other
studies.ns_score_reason: a large harmonized multisite cohort with a genuine statistical interaction, but the phenotype-mapping framing is a hard sell to general readers.
studies.the_study: Across 820 adults meeting 2016 American College of Rheumatology criteria for fibromyalgia at multiple sites, researchers examined Central Sensitization Inventory scores, Beck Depression Inventory-II scores and functional outcomes on the SF-36 and fibromyalgia impact measures. Both predictors independently tracked impairment in different domains — central sensitization with physical function, fatigue and pain; depression with emotional wellbeing and social function. Crucially, significant interactions emerged for five domains: people high on both were disproportionately impaired, beyond the sum of each.
studies.why_it_matters: Fibromyalgia is heterogeneous and contested; identifying a subgroup in whom mood and sensory amplification compound each other gives clinicians a concrete stratification and researchers a target group for mechanistic work.
studies.pitch_angle: In fibromyalgia, depression and a hypersensitive nervous system don't just add up — they multiply. Open on a patient told, as many are, that the pain is "just depression." This finding says the opposite: the two are separable, and the combination is what disables. Call Kevin Hackshaw at Dell Medical School, UT Austin.
studies.wider_angle: For a health or chronic-illness outlet: central sensitization as an emerging unifying concept across fibromyalgia, long COVID, IBS and chronic fatigue — what the construct explains, and the criticism that it risks becoming an unfalsifiable label for anything medicine can't measure.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational (cannot establish causation or direction); harmonized multisite cohort means measurement heterogeneity; all key measures self-reported questionnaires; no biological markers despite the mechanistic framing; fibromyalgia cohorts are heavily female and may not generalize.

studies.title: Resilience and social support don't independently protect refugees from PTSD
studies.ns_score_reason: a null on two of the most cited protective factors in refugee mental health, plus an unusual severity-graded analysis; cross-sectional design caps it.
studies.the_study: 461 adult Syrian refugees in Türkiye (mean age 41.5; 73.5% women) completed measures of PTSD, depression, anxiety, emotion regulation, cumulative trauma, resilience and perceived social support, analyzed by quantile regression across the full severity distribution rather than at the mean. Depression and anxiety correlated with PTSD at every quantile. Cognitive reappraisal was more strongly protective at high symptom levels; expressive suppression more strongly linked to severe symptoms. Resilience and perceived social support showed no independent association once emotional distress and trauma exposure were accounted for.
studies.why_it_matters: Resilience-building and social-support programs dominate humanitarian mental health provision; this suggests their apparent protective effect may be largely explained by the absence of distress rather than an independent buffer — though only prospective data could confirm that.
studies.pitch_angle: "Resilience" is the organizing word of refugee mental health programming. In 461 Syrian refugees, it did no independent statistical work. Open on the gap between what aid programs fund and what predicts symptoms. Call Emre Han Alpay at Mersin University. Also flag the methodological hook: averages hid the fact that emotion regulation strategies matter far more at the severe end.
studies.wider_angle: For a humanitarian or global-health outlet: the resilience industry. A reported piece on how a psychological construct became a funding category, and whether the measurement instruments (Connor-Davidson and its relatives) capture anything beyond the inverse of current distress.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation or rule out reverse direction); all self-reported; single national/refugee group in one host country; heavily female sample; resilience null may be a measurement artifact given overlap between resilience scales and low-distress items.

studies.title: Students who wrongly believe they're first-generation are the hungriest
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely odd subgroup finding, but a single mid-sized university and a cross-sectional survey keep it small.
studies.the_study: 344 students at a mid-sized US public university reported food insecurity, first-generation status (both objectively, by parental education, and subjectively, by self-identification), and depression, anxiety, stress and wellbeing. Food insecurity was the strongest predictor of all four mental health outcomes (partial η² 0.064–0.096). Neither objective nor subjective first-generation status predicted symptoms once food insecurity was accounted for — but *subjective* self-identification predicted food insecurity risk (adjusted OR 1.81) where the objective classification did not. "Over-identifiers," who called themselves first-generation despite a college-educated parent, had the highest food insecurity prevalence at 61.1%.
studies.why_it_matters: Universities target support using parental education records; this suggests a simple question about how students see themselves may identify material hardship better than the administrative category does.
studies.pitch_angle: Ask a student whether their parents went to university and you learn less about whether they're going hungry than if you just ask how they see themselves. Open on the "over-identifiers" — students with a graduate parent who nonetheless describe themselves as first-generation, and who turn out to be the most food-insecure group of all. Call Emmanuel Mutai at Purdue University Northwest. Keep it modest: this is one campus.
studies.wider_angle: For an education or social-policy outlet: campus food insecurity as an underreported driver of student mental health, and the broader question of whether objective demographic categories or subjective self-classification better identify need in welfare systems.
studies.caveats: Small-to-moderate N (344) at a single US institution; cross-sectional survey (cannot establish causation); all outcomes self-reported; the over-identifier subgroup is small; response bias likely, as food-insecure students may be over- or under-represented in voluntary surveys.

studies.title: Two rich countries, two very different routes to brain stimulation for depression
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful first cross-country comparison of how rTMS actually reaches patients, but descriptive with no patient outcomes.
studies.the_study: Investigators surveyed publicly available information from every identifiable rTMS-providing facility in Sweden and Japan for 2020–2024, extracting service distribution, registry participation, protocols, devices, practitioner roles, eligibility, reimbursement and patient counts. Sweden had 29 centers within a tax-funded regional system, near-complete national registry participation integrated with electronic health records, and predominant use of intermittent theta-burst stimulation. Japan had 112 facilities in a mixed public-private model, registry participation in only 62, and public insurance covering just one protocol — 10 Hz left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — while private clinics offered iTBS, with greater financial barriers for patients.
studies.why_it_matters: rTMS is now standard care for treatment-resistant depression in many countries, but who gets it, which protocol, and at what cost is set by reimbursement rules rather than evidence — and Japan's insurance rules effectively lock public patients out of the faster modern protocol.
studies.pitch_angle: Two wealthy countries with the same evidence base deliver brain stimulation for depression in almost opposite ways — and in one of them, the only protocol your insurance pays for is the older, slower one. Open on the difference between a 37-minute session and a 3-minute one. Call Yoshihiro Noda in Tokyo or Robert Bodén at Uppsala.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-systems or international affairs outlet: registries as invisible infrastructure. Sweden can see what happens to nearly every rTMS patient; Japan can see about half. A piece on why national treatment registries determine what any country can learn about its own care.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey of publicly available facility information, not patient-level data; no clinical outcomes; facility identification may be incomplete, particularly for private Japanese clinics; descriptive analyses only, with no formal economic evaluation; two countries cannot generalize to other health systems.

trends_raw: _No prior digest on this topic to compare against yet — this is the first run._
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** An unusual share of this batch consists of well-powered studies finding that widely funded ideas do less work than assumed once you measure them properly: resilience and perceived social support did nothing independent in 461 Syrian refugees (PMID 42642861), avatar-based VR support groups lost to a room with chairs (PMID 42661554), a perinatal depression prevention program left parental warmth unchanged at 42 months (PMID 42593980), parental problem drinking largely dissolved into co-occurring adversity in a 29-study meta-analysis (PMID 42665302), rumination turned out to have no shared EEG signature (PMID 42648371), ideology and mentalizing were displaced by ordinary distress as predictors of aggression (PMID 42661529), and the GLP-1 neuropsychiatric scare and cure narratives both failed Bradford Hill (PMID 42624955). Alongside them sit findings that explain part of the deflation — that averages hide people: the ANTOP six-year moderator analysis turning a null therapy trial into a matching rule (PMID 42611819), the multiplicative depression-by-sensitization interaction in fibromyalgia (PMID 42660390), and a subjective self-identification question outperforming the administrative category in flagging student hardship (PMID 42634162).

**Why pitch this now:** Resilience training, immersive-tech psychosocial support, two-generation perinatal programs and ACE screening are all currently absorbing large amounts of public and humanitarian money on the strength of constructs that this month's evidence suggests are either measurement artifacts of current distress or effects that only appear in identifiable subgroups.

**Angle:** A reported feature on what psychology's favorite protective factors are actually made of — following the money from funding category back to construct validity, and asking whether the field's next move is to abandon the averages and target the subgroups where effects genuinely live. Written for an educated general reader who has heard "build resilience" as advice and never asked what the word measures.

**Potential headlines:**
- Resilience, virtual reality and prevention programs are failing their own tests
- The protective factors keep vanishing once you also measure how bad people already feel
- Mental health services are being built on effects that disappear under scrutiny

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the batch is strong enough to carry a long read on measurement and construct validity without needing a single hero study, and NS readers already follow the replication story.
- **Undark** — specializes in exactly this kind of reported scrutiny of research constructs that have hardened into policy and funding categories.
- **STAT** — the clinical and reimbursement end of it (VR ventures, perinatal prevention programs, ACE screening in health systems) is squarely their beat.
- **The Guardian science desk** — the humanitarian resilience-industry strand and the UK-relevant prevention-program angle would land with their global development and health coverage.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Depression — August 2026
**Checked:** 2026-08-29 | **Studies reviewed:** 18
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-08-29

---

### Study 1: Autistic adults in the UK are twice as likely to be on antidepressants — and stay on them longer
**PMID:** 42658004 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core numbers all check out: 172,242 autistic adults (47,011 with ID, 125,231 without), 34,173,295 non-autistic adults, 30% vs 14.7% prescribed in 2023, longest course durations in the ID group, lower recording of depression/anxiety as indication in the ID group.

**Issue A. "Without a recorded mental health indication at all"** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "in the intellectual disability group frequently without a recorded mental health indication at all"
- **Abstract says:** "Recording of depression and anxiety as indications was lower for those with ID."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports *lower recording of two specific indications* (depression and anxiety) for SSRI initiation. It does not report the proportion with no recorded mental health indication of any kind — other indications (OCD, pain, sleep) could have been recorded. "Frequently without a recorded mental health indication at all" is a quantified claim the abstract does not support.
- **Suggested fix:** "and in the intellectual disability group, depression and anxiety were less often recorded as the reason for starting the drug."

**Issue B. "Last year"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Nearly one in three autistic adults in Britain was prescribed an antidepressant last year"
- **Abstract says:** "30% of autistic adults and 14.7% of non-autistic adults were prescribed an antidepressant in 2023."
- **Problem:** With a run date of August 2026, "last year" would be 2025. The data end in 2023.
- **Suggested fix:** "Nearly one in three autistic adults in Britain was prescribed an antidepressant in 2023, the most recent year in the data"

**Issue C. "Every year since 1997"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a rate that has pulled away from the general population every year since 1997"
- **Abstract says:** "Antidepressant prescribing has increased more for autistic adults than non-autistic adults since 1997"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a faster overall increase across the period, not a year-on-year widening in every single calendar year.
- **Suggested fix:** "a rate that has pulled away from the general population steadily since 1997"

**Issue D. Researcher first names** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Amir Sadik or Dhruv Rai at Bristol's MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit"
- **Abstract says:** "Sadik A(1)... Rai D(1)... MRC Integrative Epidemiology Unit... University of Bristol"
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — initials only are given. Worth checking "Dhruv Rai" against the author list before pitching; the affiliation is correct.
- **Suggested fix:** Verify given names from the published paper before use.

---

### Study 2: The eye may flag depression years early — but the layer is thicker, not thinner
**PMID:** 42637150 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 23,225 (retinal), 1,475 (eye-brain), Mendelian randomization with named GWAS datasets, positive GCIPL-depression association, mediation via primary and secondary visual cortex volumes — all accurate.

**Issue A. Prior literature characterized as a consensus for thinning** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research… the direction of effect contradicts the prevailing 'retinal thinning' story" / "Much previous work assumed neurodegeneration-style retinal thinning in depression" / "the researchers found the opposite of what the field expected"
- **Abstract says:** "previous research has yielded conflicting alterations in retinal microstructure in depression"
- **Problem:** The authors describe the prior literature as *conflicting*, not as a settled thinning consensus. The pitch hook — a reversal of what the field expected — rests on a characterization the abstract explicitly contradicts. The novelty label "Overturns prior research" inherits the same problem, and it is the main justification for the 7/10 score.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Resolves conflicting findings… Prior studies have reported contradictory retinal changes in depression; this large cohort plus Mendelian randomization points consistently toward thickening." Score revised to 6/10.

**Issue B. "Years early"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "may contain a signal about your mood years before you feel low"
- **Abstract says:** Cox regression assessing "the association between retinal microstructure and depression risk" — no follow-up duration stated.
- **Problem:** The abstract does not give a follow-up period, so "years before" is unverifiable from abstract only (plausible for UK Biobank, but needs the full text).
- **Suggested fix:** Confirm median follow-up from the paper before using "years."

---

### Study 3: Support groups in the metaverse underperform sitting in a room together
**PMID:** 42661554 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 156, three arms, four assessment points, in-person superiority for perceived social support and anxiety, avatar VR effects smaller and non-significant, attenuation at follow-up — all correctly reported.

**Issue A. Headline and pitch assert inferiority; the result is non-significance** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** Headline: "Support groups in the metaverse **underperform** sitting in a room together"; pitch: "Randomized against a room with chairs in it, the avatars lost."
- **Abstract says:** "the intervention did not show consistent superiority or equivalence to in-person groups"; "Most between-group comparisons favoured the interventions but many lacked statistical significance, probably owing to attrition and clustering."
- **Problem:** No significant VR-versus-in-person difference is reported. The trial failed to demonstrate equivalence, which is not the same as demonstrating that VR is worse. The digest's own caveat says exactly this ("findings are largely null rather than a demonstration of inferiority"), so the headline and pitch contradict the caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Metaverse support groups fail to match a room with chairs in it." Pitch: "Randomized against conventional in-person groups, the avatars couldn't demonstrate they were as good."

**Issue B. NS fit score** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10"
- **Problem:** The story value rests entirely on a null that the authors themselves attribute to attrition and clustering rather than to a true absence of effect. A 7 overstates the evidential weight of an underpowered non-significant comparison.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10, with the rationale rewritten around "first randomized head-to-head, but underpowered."

---

### Study 4: Depression compresses the mental map of emotions
**PMID:** 42658635 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Study 1 N = 1,311 aged 8–25, Study 2 N = 88 aged 18–23, 14-day experience sampling, compressed low-dimensional space, denser networks with shorter path lengths, increased transition probabilities, depression–rigid/congruent vs anxiety–unstable/incongruent, mediation abolished after controlling baseline BDI — all accurate, including the plasticity hook.

**Issue A. "Both samples Chinese students"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "both samples Chinese students, so cross-cultural generalization untested"
- **Abstract says:** "Study 1 (N = 1,311, aged 8-25)"; affiliations are Southwest University and Naval Medical University.
- **Problem:** Study 1 spans ages 8–25, so it cannot be described as a sample of students; the nationality of participants is inferred from author affiliation and is unverifiable from the abstract alone.
- **Suggested fix:** "Study 1 spans ages 8–25 and Study 2 is a small young-adult sample; both were recruited by Chinese institutions, so cross-cultural generalization is untested."

---

### Study 5: Shame — not guilt — explains why teenage girls get more depressed than boys
**PMID:** 42645734 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 2,915, mean age 16.99, 40.07% female, three waves over 12 months, females higher on all four measures, shame mediates and guilt does not, serial pathway sex → shame → maladaptive CER → depressive symptoms — all accurate.

**Issue A. Causal language for an observational mediation model** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** Headline: "Shame — not guilt — **explains why** teenage girls get more depressed"; pitch: "only the second one appears to be **making** teenage girls depressed"; Why it matters: "only one appears to **drive** the best-documented demographic gap"
- **Abstract says:** "shame mediated the sex disparity by increasing depressive risk, whereas guilt was not a significant mediator" (three-wave observational survey design)
- **Problem:** Statistical mediation in a three-wave observational study cannot establish that shame *makes* anyone depressed; it shows an association consistent with an assumed causal ordering. The digest's caveat says precisely this, so the body text contradicts the caveat. (Note the authors' own abstract uses "driven by," but a New Scientist rewrite should not amplify that.)
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Shame — not guilt — tracks the gender gap in teenage depression." Pitch: "and only the second one is statistically linked to the higher depression rates in teenage girls."

---

### Study 6: Prolonged childhood loneliness roughly triples the odds of a first psychotic episode
**PMID:** 42636467 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 2,565 (1,084 FEP, 1,481 controls), EU-GEI, LNL12 OR 2.90, independence from premorbid social isolation, LNL12-16 and affective psychosis more clearly in females, additive interaction with SCZ-PGS, MDD-PGS interaction failing the European-ancestry sensitivity analysis, and the industry disclosures for Arango, Bobes and Díaz-Caneja — all correctly captured.

**Issue A. Novelty label "New mechanism"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** New mechanism"
- **Abstract says:** An epidemiological analysis of retrospectively reported loneliness as a risk factor, with additive gene–environment interaction testing.
- **Problem:** No mechanism is identified or tested; the study reports a risk association and a statistical interaction. "New mechanism" oversells the design.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** New risk-factor evidence (gene–environment interaction)"

---

### Study 7: Thirty-seven questions predict who will still be depressed or anxious two years later
**PMID:** 42640866 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

863 items reduced to 37 via a five-step selection strategy, five algorithms, training n = 1,472 across 13 US colleges, external validation n = 823 across 13 different colleges, random forest best on discrimination/calibration/clinical utility — all accurate.

**Issue A. "One of the strongest signals" and direction ambiguity** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "can flag who will still be unwell two years later — and one of the strongest signals is simply whether the student thinks they need help"
- **Abstract says:** "Predictors of no disorders at two years included… higher feelings of calm/peacefulness, perceived need for treatment, and intention to seek help." No ranking of predictor strength is given.
- **Problem:** Two problems. First, the abstract lists predictors without ordering them, so "one of the strongest signals" is unsupported. Second, the direction is reversed in the reader's likely reading: *higher* perceived need for treatment predicted being *disorder-free*, but the sentence pairs it with "who will still be unwell."
- **Suggested fix:** "can flag who is likely to be free of all three disorders two years later — and counterintuitively, students who thought they needed treatment and intended to seek help were more likely to end up well."

**Issue B. Headline omits the eating-disorder component of the outcome** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Thirty-seven questions predict who will still be depressed or anxious two years later"
- **Abstract says:** "two-year prevention and remission of **all** anxiety, depression, and eating disorders"
- **Problem:** The outcome is a composite: free of all three conditions. Dropping eating disorders changes what the model actually predicts.
- **Suggested fix:** "Thirty-seven questions predict which students will still have an anxiety, depression or eating disorder two years on"

**Issue C. "Prediction of response"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Resist the 'AI predicts depression' framing; this is prediction of response, not diagnosis."
- **Abstract says:** The model discriminates "who did versus did not achieve two-year prevention and remission" among students receiving D-CBTgsh.
- **Problem:** With no untreated comparator in the modelling, this is prediction of *outcome* within a treated cohort, not prediction of treatment *response* in the differential sense.
- **Suggested fix:** "this predicts two-year outcome among students already receiving the digital programme, not diagnosis and not differential treatment response."

---

### Study 8: Gut bacteria in depression shift from fermenting sugars to fermenting protein
**PMID:** 42636957 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

102 MDD patients, 38 matched controls, depletion of acetate/propionate/butyrate, elevated branched-chain SCFAs, combined model of BSCFAs + acetate + API + EGF with AUC 0.871, 5-HT1A agent association — all accurate, and the caveats appropriately handle the cross-sectional design and control-group size.

**Issue A. "Run out of fiber"** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The bacteria in the gut of someone with depression appear to have run out of fiber and started breaking down protein instead"
- **Abstract says:** "a pathological shift from saccharolytic to proteolytic fermentation" — no dietary data are reported.
- **Problem:** Diet and fibre intake were not measured. Attributing the fermentation shift to fibre deficiency imports a causal dietary explanation that the study cannot distinguish from illness effects, medication, transit time or other confounders — and it sits awkwardly beside the same section's instruction not to imply anyone should change their diet.
- **Suggested fix:** "The gut bacteria of people with depression appear to be fermenting more protein and less carbohydrate, generating compounds that track with inflammation and symptom severity — though the study did not measure what anyone ate."

**Issue B. "Number of past episodes"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the same markers tracked symptom severity, physiosomatic symptoms and number of past episodes"
- **Abstract says:** "higher OSOD, more severe physiosomatic symptoms, and increased ROI [recurrence of illness]"
- **Problem:** Recurrence of illness in this research group's framework is a composite index, not simply a count of prior episodes.
- **Suggested fix:** "…and a higher recurrence-of-illness index."

---

### Study 9: Which psychotherapy works for anorexia may depend on how depressed you are
**PMID:** 42611819 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

242 randomized across 10 German university hospitals, three arms, no BMI difference, secondary analysis of N = 160 in the two active arms, MMRM with BMI at T5 (mean 5.96 years), moderation direction (low depression/high mental QoL → CBT-E; high depression/low mental QoL → FPT), consistency across T1–T4, wide middle range where treatments perform alike — all accurate and well caveated.

**Issue A. "Mattered a great deal"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Six years on, the data say it mattered a great deal — if you were also depressed."
- **Abstract says:** "Graphical visualisation confirms that there is a wide range where both treatments perform similarly, while CBT or FPT perform differently in the extreme ranges of these two variables."
- **Problem:** No effect sizes for the moderation are given, and the abstract stresses that the differentiation appears only at the extremes. "A great deal" implies a magnitude the abstract does not support.
- **Suggested fix:** "Six years on, the data say it may have mattered — for patients at the depressed end of the range."

---

### Study 10: Stress and low mood predict everyday aggression; political ideology doesn't
**PMID:** 42661529 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 1,215, predictor set, unique associations for stress/anxiety/depressive symptoms, distress block explaining the largest share of variance, null for mentalizing and RWA facets, small inverse SDO association interpreted cautiously, robust and quantile regression support — all accurate.

**Issue A. Content of the aggression index is invented** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "what actually predicted having hit, shoved or shouted at someone recently"
- **Abstract says:** "recent aggressive behavior using a brief aggression index" — items are not described.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only; the specific acts are the writer's illustration, not the measure's content.
- **Suggested fix:** "what actually predicted recent aggressive acts" — or confirm the item content from the full text before specifying behaviours.

**Issue B. Sample nationality** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "French community sample only"
- **Abstract says:** "In a community sample of adults (N = 1,215)" — no country stated; the sole author is affiliated with French institutions.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. Reasonable inference, but it should be confirmed rather than asserted in a caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "Single community sample, country of recruitment to be confirmed from the full text."

---

### Study 11: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and the brain: the causal evidence isn't there yet
**PMID:** 42624955 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The Bradford Hill framing, the evidence sources (receptor pharmacology, preclinical, RCTs, observational and pharmacovigilance), the outcome list (depression, anxiety, suicidality, reward-related behaviour, cognition, ocular disturbance) and the conclusion — plausibility yes, causality insufficient — all match the abstract. The review status is disclosed in the score rationale and the caveats.

---

### Study 12: Rumination has no shared brain signature — everyone ruminates differently
**PMID:** 42648371 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 24 depressed participants, six eight-minute inductions across three sessions, 64-channel EEG, participant-specific linear SVMs on alpha/beta/theta plus inter-channel connectivity, small-but-significant group-average accuracy, 10 of 24 above chance, heterogeneous feature weights — all accurate.

**Issue A. Ground truth mislabelled** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "self-reported rumination levels as the ground truth"
- **Abstract says:** "We used validated tasks to induce rumination or distraction… we trained participant-specific linear support vector machines to differentiate state rumination from distraction… and measured self-reported levels of rumination."
- **Problem:** The classification labels were the induced conditions (rumination vs distraction task); self-report served as a manipulation check ("Participants reported strongly increased rumination"), not as the classifier's ground truth.
- **Suggested fix:** "labels came from the induction condition rather than from spontaneous rumination, with self-report used only as a manipulation check."

**Issue B. Headline absolutism** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Rumination has **no** shared brain signature"
- **Abstract says:** "averaged across all participant-specific decoders we classified state rumination from EEG patterns with small albeit significant accuracy… variability in ruminative processes limits the generalization of decoding approaches across participants."
- **Problem:** There was a small but statistically significant signal on average; the finding is heterogeneity limiting generalization, not the total absence of a shared signature.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rumination has no reliable shared brain signature — everyone ruminates differently"

---

### Study 13: Growing up with a parent's drinking problem raises adult depression risk — but not on its own
**PMID:** 42665302 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

32 studies eligible, 29 meta-analysed, four databases, anxiety SMD 0.37 / 73% higher likelihood, depression SMD 0.29 / 65% higher likelihood, attenuation but retained significance in confounder-adjusted studies — all accurate.

**Issue A. "Much of" / "substantially shared" overstates "partly explained"** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the authors conclude that much of the association may reflect co-occurring childhood adversities and broader family dysfunction" / "the mental health risk is real but substantially shared with other family adversity"
- **Abstract says:** "these associations may be **partly** explained by co-occurring childhood adversities and broader family dysfunction"
- **Problem:** "Much of" and "substantially" quantify an attribution the authors deliberately left unquantified, and the abstract notes the associations *remained statistically significant* after adjustment. The deflationary framing — which is the whole hook of the entry — is stronger than the source supports.
- **Suggested fix:** "the authors conclude the association may be partly explained by co-occurring childhood adversities and broader family dysfunction" / "the mental health risk is real, and partly shared with other family adversity."

---

### Study 14: Preventing perinatal depression doesn't automatically make parents warmer
**PMID:** 42593980 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 103 dyads, MB versus community home-visiting care as usual, 42 months postpartum, virtual observational coding with the Brief Parent-Child Early Relational Assessment, no significant differences in amount or quality of verbal and physical warmth, and the authors' own suggestion that parenting may need direct targeting — all match. The caveats correctly note that this is a substudy of a longitudinal observational study rather than the original randomized comparison, and flag possible underpowering.

---

### Study 15: In fibromyalgia, depression and body-wide symptom burden multiply each other
**PMID:** 42660390 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

820 adults, 2016 ACR criteria, CSI/BDI-II/SF-36/FIQR, significant CSI × BDI interactions in five domains (Role Physical, Role Emotional, Energy/Fatigue, Emotional Well-Being, Social Functioning), greatest impairment in those elevated on both — all accurate.

**Issue A. "Different domains" understates the overlap** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Both predictors independently tracked impairment in different domains — central sensitization with physical function, fatigue and pain; depression with emotional wellbeing and social function."
- **Abstract says:** CSI with Physical Functioning, Energy/Fatigue, Pain, General Health; depressive symptoms with Emotional Well-Being, Social Functioning, **Physical Functioning**, and Health Change.
- **Problem:** Depression was also independently associated with Physical Functioning, so the clean "sensory vs emotional" split implied by "different domains" is not what the model showed.
- **Suggested fix:** "Both predictors independently tracked impairment, with partly distinct profiles — central sensitization strongest for pain, fatigue and general health; depression strongest for emotional wellbeing and social function, though it also predicted physical functioning."

---

### Study 16: Resilience and social support don't independently protect refugees from PTSD
**PMID:** 42642861 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N = 461 Syrian refugees in Türkiye, mean age 41.54, 73.5% women, quantile regression across the symptom distribution, depression and anxiety associated at all quantiles, cognitive reappraisal more strongly inverse at high symptom levels, expressive suppression more strongly linked to severe symptoms, and resilience and perceived social support not independently associated after accounting for emotional distress and cumulative trauma. The "Why it matters" section is appropriately hedged ("only prospective data could confirm that") and the caveats cover the cross-sectional design and the possible measurement artefact.

---

### Study 17: Students who wrongly believe they're first-generation are the hungriest
**PMID:** 42634162 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 344 at a mid-sized public university, partial η² 0.064–0.096, neither objective nor subjective first-generation status predicting symptoms after accounting for food insecurity, subjective identification predicting food insecurity risk (aOR 1.81) where objective classification did not, over-identifiers at 61.1% — all accurate.

**Issue A. "Wrongly believe"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "Students who **wrongly** believe they're first-generation are the hungriest"
- **Abstract says:** "'Over-identifiers'—students who self-identified as first-generation despite having a college-educated parent"
- **Problem:** The abstract describes a mismatch with the parental-education definition, not an error of fact by the student; definitions of "first-generation" vary (foreign degrees, non-completing parents, two-year vs four-year institutions). "Wrongly" editorializes, and it sits oddly against the entry's own argument that the subjective measure identifies need better than the administrative category.
- **Suggested fix:** "Students who call themselves first-generation — even when a parent has a degree — are the hungriest"

---

### Study 18: Two rich countries, two very different routes to brain stimulation for depression
**PMID:** 42658152 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

29 Swedish centres, near-complete registry participation integrated with EHRs, iTBS predominance, 112 Japanese facilities, 62 in the registry, public insurance covering only 10 Hz left DLPFC, iTBS in private clinics, greater financial barriers in Japan — all accurate, and the caveats correctly note the descriptive design and absence of patient-level or economic data.

**Issue A. Session-duration detail not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Open on the difference between a 37-minute session and a 3-minute one."
- **Abstract says:** Protocols are named (10 Hz left DLPFC; iTBS) but no session durations are reported.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. The figures are conventional for the two protocols but are external context, not a study finding.
- **Suggested fix:** Attribute the durations to standard protocol references rather than to this paper.

**Issue B. "Standard care… in many countries"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "rTMS is now standard care for treatment-resistant depression in many countries"
- **Abstract says:** "rTMS is an evidence-based intervention for major depressive disorder (MDD) and treatment-resistant depression (TRD)."
- **Problem:** The study covers two countries; the abstract characterizes rTMS as evidence-based, not as standard care internationally.
- **Suggested fix:** "rTMS is an evidence-based treatment for treatment-resistant depression, but who gets it, which protocol, and at what cost is set by reimbursement rules rather than evidence."

---

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Autistic adults twice as likely to be on antidepressants | ⚠️ Minor issues | "No recorded indication" overstated (Mod); "last year" = 2023; "every year since 1997"; author first names unverified |
| 2 | The eye may flag depression years early | ⚠️ Minor issues | Prior literature was "conflicting," not a thinning consensus (Mod) — undercuts "Overturns prior research" and the 7/10; "years early" unverifiable |
| 3 | Support groups in the metaverse underperform | ⚠️ Minor issues | Headline/pitch assert inferiority from a non-significant result, contradicting own caveat (Mod); score 7 → 6 |
| 4 | Depression compresses the mental map of emotions | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Both samples Chinese students" — Study 1 is aged 8–25; nationality inferred |
| 5 | Shame — not guilt — explains teenage girls' depression | ⚠️ Minor issues | Causal language ("explains why," "making," "drive") for observational mediation (Mod) |
| 6 | Childhood loneliness triples odds of first psychosis | ⚠️ Minor issues | "New mechanism" label doesn't fit a risk-factor/interaction analysis |
| 7 | Thirty-seven questions predict two-year outcome | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Strongest signal" unranked + direction ambiguity on perceived need (Mod); headline drops eating disorders; "response" vs outcome |
| 8 | Gut bacteria shift to fermenting protein | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Run out of fiber" — diet not measured (Mod); recurrence-of-illness index ≠ number of episodes |
| 9 | Which anorexia therapy works may depend on depression | ⚠️ Minor issues | "Mattered a great deal" overstates an extremes-only exploratory moderator |
| 10 | Distress, not ideology, predicts aggression | ⚠️ Minor issues | Aggression-index content invented; sample nationality unverifiable |
